name: Kata Containers
summary: An OCI- and CRI-compatible container runtime that maps container workloads into lightweight hardware-virtualized sandboxes with a guest kernel, agent, hypervisor, and paravirtualized devices.

features.name: VM-backed sandbox boundary
features.description: Kata replaces the host-kernel process boundary used by a conventional runtime with a lightweight VM and guest Linux kernel; containers run inside the VM while the host and guest kernels remain separate.
benefits: Adds a hardware-virtualized boundary around the guest kernel and workloads
Preserves a container-oriented interface for callers
costs: Requires a guest kernel, VMM, and virtualization support
Adds startup, memory, and device-mediation overhead relative to host processes

features.name: Shim, agent, and hypervisor composition
features.description: The containerd shim launches and manages a Kata sandbox, while the guest agent and selected hypervisor cooperate to create and operate the VM-backed container environment.
benefits: Integrates VM lifecycle with existing containerd and CRI runtime selection
Allows multiple hypervisor implementations behind a runtime configuration
costs: Failures cross host, shim, VMM, guest agent, and guest-kernel boundaries
Runtime configuration must coordinate several independently evolving components

features.name: CRI-to-virtual-device mapping
features.description: Kata maps CRI constructs such as pod sandboxes, containers, networks, storage, and resource constraints to VMs, guest processes and namespaces, virtual NICs, virtual storage, and vCPU or memory resources.
benefits: Makes VM-backed isolation usable through common container APIs
Provides explicit device boundaries for network, storage, and guest communication
costs: Compatibility depends on the selected VMM and available virtual devices
Device translation can add latency and configuration constraints

mathematical_views.question: How does a container or pod request refine through a shim into a VM, guest kernel, and guest workload?
assumptions: The host runtime, VM, guest kernel, and workload are separate layers
The model treats hardware virtualization as an isolation boundary, not as a proof of security
Each layer exposes only the resource and lifecycle interface needed by the next layer

mathematical_views.question: Which VM resources and virtual devices represent each CRI-level workload construct?
assumptions: CRI constructs and VM resources are modeled as typed nodes
The mapping abstracts VMM-specific implementation differences
The model does not claim all CRI features have identical behavior across hypervisors

mathematical_views.question: How do shim, VM, agent, and guest container states advance together during create, start, and teardown?
assumptions: The shim owns the external lifecycle contract
VM and agent readiness are explicit intermediate states
The model leaves restart and partial-failure recovery as validation gaps

benefits: Stronger separation from the host kernel than a native process container
Container-compatible control surface over selectable VM implementations
costs: More components and cross-boundary failure handling

benefits: Explicit and portable resource translation model
costs: Virtual device compatibility and performance depend on configuration
